newsitem.title: FRENCH GUIANA: Ariane rocket launches U.S. communications satellite.
newsitem.headline: Ariane rocket launches U.S. communications satellite.

text.p: Western Europe's 91st Ariane rocket blasted off from equatorial French Guiana late on Tuesday and placed into orbit a U.S. direct broadcast telecommunications satellite.
The Ariane 42P rocket equipped with two solid strap-on boosters lifted off at at 9.00 p.m. local French Guiana time (0000 GMT Wednesday) into a clear equatorial night sky.

Twenty minutes after takeoff space officials said the ECHOSTAR-2 satellite separated from the rocket. The 2.8 tonne satellite will provide direct-to-home satellite television, audio and data broadcasting throughout the continental United States for the Colorado-based Echostar Communications Corp DISH .
"We see direct satellite broadcasting increasing dramatically in North America. It is by far the most efficient broadcasting mode," Charlie Ergen Echostar president told Reuters.
"Our objective is to put a (satellite) dish in every home, school and business in America," he said.
Ergen said the cost of ECHOSTAR-2 -- satellite, launch and insurance was $225 million.
Major users of Echostar satellites include HBO, CNN, Turner Broadcasting. Consumers can capture Echostar broadcasting using 18 inch satellite dishes.
Echostar said their satellite broadcasts will be equipped with "V-chip technology" that will allow viewers to block certain channels or specific programs.
"Programming can ... be blocked at four content levels including violence, language, nudity and sexual content," the company said in a statement.
The satellite was built by Lockheed Martin unit Lockheed Martin Astro Space and is designed to operate in space for 10 years.
Originally slated for launch aboard a Chinese Long March rocket, the company switched to the European Ariane earlier this year, in the aftermath of several failures of Long March in China.

Tuesday's launch was the fourth Ariane mission since the disasterous failure on June 4 of an Ariane-5 rocket, the first of a new generation, less than 40 seconds after its maiden launch from the European Space Agency launch center in Kourou, French Guiana on the northeast coast of South America.
An investigation panel concluded in July that design errors in the software of the rocket's guidance system was the cause of the failure.

It was the ninth Ariane-4 successfully launched this year by the Paris-based Ariane space company that controls more than half of the world's commercial satellite launch market with firm orders to launch 41 satellites worth an estimated $4 billion.
